newsitem.title: USA: Reader's Digest to face Yahoo! on Intenet.
newsitem.headline: Reader's Digest to face Yahoo! on Intenet.

text.p: Reader's Digest Association Inc on Tuesday will launch LookSmart, an Internet search service meant to tidy up the unruly World Wide Web and make it presentable for millions of mainstream consumers.

The direct-selling and publishing group, whose Reader's Digest magazine culls the world of print for its 27 million monthly subscribers, said its LookSmart search service will rank and sort some 85,000 sites more sensibibly for a mass audience than such rivals as Infoseek and Yahoo! Inc.
Yahoo and Infoseek are both search engines for seeking out information on the Internet's World Wide Web of computer networks.
Reuters New Media, a unit of international news and information organisation Reuters Holdings Plc, has a small stake in Yahoo! and supplies it with news.

Executives of Reader's Digest said LookSmart, and a companion Reader's Digest World site, will be promoted in the company's magazines, online and in the 500 million pieces of junk mail it dispatches each year to potential buyers of Reader's Digest videos, recordings and books.
Both LookSmart and Reader's Digest World site will launch on October 28.

Reader's Digest also wants joint marketing ventures for LookSmart, similar to ones Reader's Digest has in place with lifestyle-publisher Meredith Corp and cosmetics-giant Avon Products Inc, Sarah Hamman, director of the company's new media projects, said during an interview.
She declined to discuss specifics of any such possible deals.

What Reader's Digest magazine does with magazines, newspapers and books, LookSmart will do on the World Wide Web, culling and evaluating sites from the hundreds of thousands available on the Web. The service will make it more simple to reach the best of them, LookSmart President Evan Thornley said.

" What most users want most of the time is organization of the (sites) into categories," he said. "The people with jobs and mortgages ... that's the majority of people. They want a web that helps meet their needs."

LookSmart, a majority-owned subsidiary of Reader's Digest Association, expects advertising to provide nearly all its revenues. Technology companies would be the first sponsors, eventually to be followed by consumer-brand companies as the Internet becomes a mass medium, Thornley said.

Unlike other search engines, or online catologs of websites, LookSmart's displays will fill only one full screen and will need no scrolling. Advertisements will be fixed on the bottom one-eighth of the user's screen, Thornley said.
LookSmart's revenues were likely to match or exceed those of similar search engines, running at about a $10 million annual pace in the first half of 1996, Thornley said.
Hamman said LookSmart would provide Reader's Digest, whose whose biggest businesses are selling books and other entertainment by mail, with a new sales outlet.
"This gives us another gateway to customers," she said.

The company's second site, Reader's Digest World, will contain material from Reader's Digest magazine, information from the company's special-interest and improvement books, and an electronic outlet for buy any of some 300 products Reader's Digest will offer online.
